facts.fact: In the UK the Writers’ Guild of Great Britain negotiates minimum terms agreements for writers in TV, theatre, audio and some film, and a writer or agent may negotiate above them.

Under the BBC/PMA/WGGB television script agreement from 15 December 2025 the minimum for a teleplay is £239 a minute (£14,340 per 60 minutes) and for series and serials £220 a minute (£13,200 per 60 minutes).
The BBC television writers’ attendance fee is £128 from 15 December 2025.

Under the ITV/WGGB/PMA agreement from 19 October 2026 the minimum script fee is £16,460 per hour of slot length for an original teleplay, £12,882 per hour for series and serials, and £4,294 per half hour for a long-running series, pro rata.
The ITV writers’ attendance fee is £140 a day from 19 October 2026.

The PACT/WGGB film schedule still published by the Guild sets a total guaranteed payment of £42,120 for a feature budgeted at £2 million and over, paid in stages from treatment to principal photography, and the total minimum payment buys all the rights.
Directors UK, the directors’ body in the UK, has over 8,500 members and distributes rights payments to them.
Equity is the UK performers’ union; a performer need not be a member to work on Equity-agreed rates, but only members vote on offers.
Equity’s subscription from February 2025 is £16.50 a month for members earning up to £40,000 a year.
Equity student membership costs £3.60 a month, and graduates earning under £40,000 pay a subsidised rate for up to two years after their course.
Under the Equity/PACT Cinema Film Agreement (2021 version) minors aged 10 to school-leaving age are guaranteed at least 50% of adult minimum fees, and use fees total 280% across the markets.
The Equity/BBC TV agreement raised minimum episodic fees by 13% from 7 April 2025.
Equity advises that a UK agent may not charge up-front fees and must pass on a performer’s fees within 10 days of receiving them.
UK productions claim the Audio-Visual Expenditure Credit at 34% of qualifying expenditure, 39% for children’s and animated work, and 53% for independent films.
An independent film for the 53% rate must have core costs under £23.5 million and may claim on up to £15 million of core costs.
A high-end TV programme qualifies only with average core costs of at least £1 million per hour of slot length.
Every film or programme claiming the credit must be certified British by the BFI through the cultural test or a co-production treaty.
UK spend on film and high-end TV production was £6.8 billion in 2025; 193 films and 168 HETV productions started.
Domestic UK features accounted for £193 million, or 7%, of UK film production spend in 2025.

In England, Wales and Scotland a child (under 16, compulsory school age) may not perform in a broadcast, filmed or paid performance without a licence from the local authority, unless unpaid and on no more than three days in six months.
An English local authority may refuse a child performance licence applied for less than 21 days before the first performance.
In England and Wales a person attains full age at 18.

The Writers Guild of Canada’s agreements with independent producers cover all English-language production in Canada, setting minimum fees and distribution payments; the WGC/CMPA IPA runs from 22 May 2024 to 31 January 2027.
Under the WGC/CMPA IPA the minimum fee for a feature film script is $71,202 CAD from 1 February 2026 (a polish $10,664).
Under the WGC/CMPA IPA the minimum for a series script of 30 minutes or less is $10,546 CAD and of 60 minutes or less $21,088 CAD from 1 February 2026.
To join the WGC a writer submits a fully signed writing contract with a producer not older than two years, and pays annual basic dues of $175 CAD.
ACTRA’s Independent Production Agreement covers performers in film, TV and digital media across Canada except British Columbia, which has its own agreement through UBCP/ACTRA.
Under the 2025-2027 ACTRA IPA a principal actor’s minimum is $972.75 CAD a day ($4,133.50 a week) in 2026 and $1,006.75 a day in 2027.
Under the 2025-2027 ACTRA IPA an actor (the smaller-part category) earns at least $656.50 CAD a day in 2026, and a background performer $284.50 a day.
Full ACTRA membership costs a one-time $1,600 CAD initiation fee plus $195 a year and working dues of 2.25% of gross earnings, up to $4,000 a year combined.
A performer becomes an ACTRA apprentice with one qualifying work permit (not a background permit) for a $75 CAD yearly fee, and full ACTRA members may not accept non-union work.
The federal Canadian Film or Video Production Tax Credit is fully refundable at 25% of qualified labour expenditure.
Qualified labour may not exceed 60% of production cost net of assistance, so the credit is at most 15% of that cost.

A Canadian production needs at least 6 of 10 key creative points (director 2, screenwriter 2, the two highest-paid lead performers 1 each, plus four crew posts at 1 each), with a Canadian director or screenwriter and a Canadian lead.
The producer, co-producer, line producer and production manager on a CPTC production must be Canadian.
Telefilm Canada administered $148.4 million in 2025-2026 and supported 126 new feature films, 31 of them official co-productions.
Telefilm’s Talent to Watch program finances emerging filmmakers’ first features, putting $3,598,068 CAD into 16 projects in 2026-27 against $31,242,084 requested.
The Canadian Screen Awards’ 2027 film acting categories are Performance in a Leading Role and Performance in a Supporting Role (each in drama and comedy), not split by sex.
In Ontario an employer must hold 25% of a child performer’s earnings over $2,000 on a production in trust until the child turns 18.
In Ontario a child performer may not work more than eight hours a day, and one under 16 must be accompanied to and from work by a parent, guardian or authorized chaperone.
In Ontario the age of majority is 18.
Under the French cinema production collective agreement an actor’s minimum was €418.25 per day engagement (cachet) and €1,266.70 for a five-day week from September 2023.
Under that agreement a third of the actor’s base pay buys the exploitation rights, split 37% for cinemas, 25% for TV, 10% for on-demand, 15% for video and 13% for other uses.
A French performer qualifies for intermittent unemployment benefit (annex 10) with 507 hours in the 12 months before the contract taken, each cachet counting as 12 hours.
The intermittent benefit for artists is at least €44 a day and at most €174.80 a day (since 1 January 2024).
France’s cinema and audiovisual tax credit is 20% of eligible French spending, 25% for TV fiction and animation, and 30% for animated films and films made mainly in French or a regional language.
The tax credits on one cinema work may not exceed €30 million.
The CNC approved (agréé) 290 films in 2025, French cinemas sold 156.2 million tickets, and French films took 37.9% of the market.
The CNC paid €772.4 million in support in 2025, €315.5 million of it for cinema and €283.0 million for audiovisual.
The César awards split acting by sex: Best Actress, Best Actor, the two supporting categories and Most Promising Actress and Actor.

facts.fact: The César Révélations list of up to sixteen actresses and sixteen actors draws from performers aged at least 15 in the ceremony year.

Membership of the César Academy is open to adults in French cinema backed by two member sponsors, e.g. a director with two features in ten years, or an actor with five features in roles 1 to 10 (or three in roles 1 to 3) in five years.
The César categories for writers and directors are Best Original Screenplay, Best Adaptation and Best Direction.

Every film for public exhibition in India is certified by the CBFC as U (unrestricted), UA with an age advisory of 7+, 13+ or 16+, A (adults only) or S (restricted to a profession or class of persons), under the Cinematograph (Certification) Rules 2024.
FWICE, the Federation of Western India Cine Employees, is the film industry workers’ union in Mumbai.
The Filmfare Awards split acting by sex: Best Actor in a Leading Role (Female) and (Male), and the same for supporting roles.

India’s Child and Adolescent Labour Act 2016 bars child employment but lets a child work as an artist in audio-visual entertainment under the rules’ conditions, and every screening must carry a disclaimer that no child was abused, neglected or exploited in the shoot.

Germany’s DFFF I grant pays a German-based producer up to 30% of recognised German production costs, capped at €5 million, for cinema features costing at least €1 million (documentaries €200,000, animation €2 million).
A DFFF I application needs 45% of the financing closed to be filed and 65% to be granted, and the producer must have released at least one feature in German cinemas.
For 2026 shoots the DFFF I closed after its planned €30 million of applications was reached.
An international co-production must spend at least 25% of its total costs in Germany to receive the DFFF I.
Membership of BFFS, the German actors’ union, costs €180 a year on gross earnings up to €50,000, €320 between €50,000 and €90,000, €450 above that, and €50 for drama students, plus a €50 joining fee.
The Deutscher Filmpreis splits acting by sex: Best Female and Best Male Leading Role and Supporting Role, alongside Best Direction and Best Screenplay.

In Germany a child may act in film only with the labour inspectorate’s written approval, children over three to six for up to two hours a day between 8 and 17, and over six for up to three hours between 8 and 22.
A German child performer must have at least 14 hours uninterrupted rest after the work.
In Germany majority begins at 18.
Australia’s Producer Offset is a refundable tax offset of 40% of qualifying Australian production expenditure for a cinema feature and 30% for TV or streaming projects shot from 1 July 2021.
A Producer Offset project must have significant Australian content or be an official co-production, and is claimed in the producer’s tax return for the year the project is completed.
Screen Australia’s final certificate fee runs from A$168 for QAPE up to A$1 million to A$5,884 above A$30 million.
The Australian Directors’ Guild recommends a minimum weekly fee for a series director of A$4,000 (low budget), A$6,000 (mid) or A$8,000 (high budget), by budget per episode, plus superannuation.
The ADG card gives a series director as many weeks of prep as of shoot, two more for a set-up or pilot director, and 3 days of editing per half-hour episode (5 per hour) for a director’s cut.
Under the ADG card the director who directs most of an episode gets a sole “Directed by” credit, and overtime applies past a 12-hour shoot day.
Full membership of the Australian Writers’ Guild needs produced screen, stage, audio or interactive writing; associate membership is for unproduced writers.
AWG full membership costs A$325 a year on income under A$40,000, rising to A$850 over A$100,000, plus a one-off A$185 joining fee.
Japanese cinemas sold 188.756 million tickets in 2025 for ¥274.452 billion, with 1,305 releases (694 Japanese) on 3,697 screens.
The Japan Academy Film Prize splits leading and supporting acting by sex (主演男優賞, 主演女優賞, 助演女優賞 and so on) and gives a newcomer award (新人俳優賞) to actors of either sex.

Japan’s Labour Standards Act bars employing a child before the first 31 March after age 15, but with the labour office’s permission a child of any age may work in film or theatre outside school hours.
In Japan adulthood begins at 18.

KOFIC’s co-production fund (annual budget KRW 3 billion) pays up to 50% of the Korean company’s net production cost, at most KRW 500 million, on a feature co-production where each country puts in 20% to 80%.
Under KOFIC’s co-production fund, spending on main cast beyond 50% of total labour costs is not counted.
Nigeria’s National Film and Video Censors Board classifies every film shown in Nigeria and licenses its distributors and exhibitors.
NFVCB classes are G, PG, 12, 12A, 15, 18 and RE (restricted exhibition).
NFVCB classification of a 91-120 minute film costs ₦45,000 in a local language, ₦60,000 in English or ₦70,000 if foreign, plus 30% for public exhibition and ₦50,000 for fast track.
Spain gives investors in Spanish films and series a tax deduction of 30% of the first €1 million and 25% above it, capped at €20 million per film and €10 million per series episode.
At least 50% of the deduction base must be spent in Spain, and the work needs a nationality and cultural certificate from the ICAA or its regional counterpart.
The Goya awards split acting by sex: lead, supporting and newcomer actress and actor, and give a best new director award.
In Spain majority begins at 18.
The David di Donatello split acting by sex (best lead and supporting actress and actor) and include best first feature (esordio alla regia).
Academy members become David di Donatello jurors by paying €90 for the 2027 edition.
Mexico’s EFICINE (Income Tax Law art. 189) gives taxpayers a credit for what they put into national film production, up to 10% of the previous year’s income tax.
EFICINE may not exceed MXN 20 million per taxpayer per production project, and its total for production is capped at MXN 650 million a year.
Ireland’s Section 481 film tax credit is 32% of the lowest of eligible expenditure, 80% of qualifying production costs or €125 million (for projects certified from 28 March 2024).
The producer applies to the Minister before the film starts, and may claim up to 90% of the credit on budgeted spending with the rest on completion.

South Africa’s SA Film & TV production incentive is 35% of qualifying South African production expenditure, plus 5% with at least 20% Black South African heads of department, up to R25 million a project.
A South African production needs QSAPE of at least R2.5 million (R500,000 for documentaries), half its principal photography in South Africa, and 25% of its budget committed when applying.

sources.title: Screen Australia: Producer Offset
sources.said: The Producer Offset is a refundable tax offset (rebate) for producers of Australian screen content. It is calculated on a completed project’s qualifying Australian production expenditure (QAPE). ... 40% of an applicant’s QAPE for a feature film that was produced for commercial exhibition to the public in cinemas; ... 30% of an applicant’s QAPE for an eligible project produced for television or a subscription service, where the project commenced principal photography on or after 1 July 2021. ... have significant Australian content (SAC) or be an Official Co-production made under one of the current Arrangements: ... no more than $1,000,000 = $168 ... more than $30,000,000 = $5,884 ... The applicant then claims the Producer Offset in the applicant’s income tax return to the ATO for the financial year in which the project is completed.

sources.title: Revenue (Ireland): Film Relief (Section 481 Film Tax Credit)
sources.said: The credit is 32% of whichever is the lowest of: eligible expenditure 80% of total qualifying film production costs or €125 million. ... This new maximum expenditure amount of €125 million applies to projects certified on or after 28 March 2024. ... You can claim the credit in full after the film is completed. Alternatively, you can claim for up to 90% of the credit based on budgeted expenditure with the balance claimed on completion.
